events.text: Day 1 begins.

Morning. Let me get straight to it: I'm thinking Omar (p6) is the one worth examining today.

Day one, nobody has any real information, so people will be tempted to pick names at random. I'm not going to do that. Here's my reasoning: Omar, your first public move was a very quick, very clean read of the table — the kind of thing that looks like good instincts but could equally be someone who already knows how the night went. A pure villager guessing would usually be a little messier than that. That calmness is what put you on my list, not any single word you said.

I also want to be honest about my own position: I have no investigation results and I'm not going to pretend otherwise. I'm voting on behavior and on how you framed the group, and that's it.

Before we vote, I'd like to hear one thing from Omar: which living player do you consider the biggest threat to the town right now, and why? If your answer lines up with what you'd have said at night, that tells me something too.

Felix, you're welcome to scrutinize me — but let me push back on your logic, because it cuts both ways. You say I was "too clean" with my reads. Then you immediately come out on Day 1 with a confident, well-structured case against me. By your own standard, shouldn't that make you suspicious too? Anyone can prepare a polished accusation in advance.

You asked me which living player I consider the biggest threat to the town right now, so I'll answer honestly: I'd want more conversation before naming a definitive threat — but if pressed, I'd point to players who are already building early voting coalitions based on thin evidence rather than waiting to hear everyone speak. Day 1 accusations with no real information are exactly how mafia towns mislead each other.

I'll be transparent about one thing: I have no investigation results to share, and I'm not going to bluff about one. I'm judging behavior only, same as everyone else.

Felix — you directed your sharpest question at me, so I'll direct this back to you: you said you're voting on "behavior and how I framed the group." What specifically did I say about the group that you think a mafia member would say but a villager wouldn't? I want you to point to the actual words, not a vibe. If your case is real, you should be able to be precise about it.

Omar, you asked me to point to actual words rather than a vibe, so here they are — and I'll be careful to answer the question you actually asked.

I said two things: that your opening read of the table was "too clean," and that you framed the group as a set of people tempted to "pick names at random." My case was never that you said something mafia-only. It was that you delivered a confident read before anyone had spoken, and that calmness was the thing worth examining. That's a behavior claim, and you asked me to defend it — so: a villager's first read is usually a bit messy, because a villager doesn't know what the night produced. A player who already knows how the night went can be smooth, because there's no surprise in the information.

Now your answer, and this is the part that actually matters: you were asked which living player you consider the biggest threat to the town, and you named nobody. You said you'd want more conversation. You then spent the rest of the message explaining why naming names would be a mistake, and you described me — the only person who had accused anyone — as part of a "coalition." So the rule you've applied is: I must produce a specific accusation, and if you don't, you get to call it a pattern. That asymmetry is the tell, Omar. Not the vocabulary.

You also never once said what you saw at night, and you never said you saw nothing at night either. I told you plainly that I have no investigation results. You noticed that. You chose not to make it reciprocal.

And for the record: telling me that a polished accusation might be prepared in advance is not a defense of you, it's an attack on every player who has the confidence to make one. If the standard is "don't be too sure too early," then Isha, Maya, Sam and Leo are all suspect under it too — and I'd rather we examine that standard than accept it from the one player who hasn't named a target.

I'm still examining you, Omar. Say something specific.

Let me take the remaining part of my turn and then I'll get out of the way.

Omar asked me to point to actual words, and I did. My case against him was never "he said something mafia-only" — it was that he declined to answer a direct question and then turned the refusal into an accusation. That's still where I am, and I'll be honest that I'm not certain. It's Day 1. I could be wrong.

But here's the thing that actually decides it. When I asked which living player he considers the biggest threat, Omar gave me a category, not a person. "Players who are building early voting coalitions based on thin evidence." That's a description of me, dressed as a principle. If a rule is "anyone who accuses early is suspect," then I'm already a suspect under it, and so is anyone else who speaks up before there's information. That's a rule that makes accusation itself dangerous to the town — and it was proposed by the one player here who hasn't named a target. Meanwhile the night: I said plainly that I have no investigation results. Omar heard that, said nothing about his own night, and never once said he saw nothing either. Every honest player can say "I saw nothing" or "I have something." Omar said neither.

So, Omar, one last time and I'll stop asking: name one living player — one name — who you consider the biggest threat to the town right now, and say what you saw at night: nothing, or something. If you give me a name and a night statement, my case against you weakens and I'll say so in the vote. If you give me another principle about how accusations work, then the vote is straightforward, because a player who won't say who they think is dangerous is dangerous in exactly the way that costs the town a night.

To everyone else: I've used up my time on theory. If you have any information at all from last night — anything, even "I saw nothing and it was quiet" — say it out loud now, because that's the only currency we have today. And if you're sitting on a real result, the town needs it more than it needs another speech about voting standards.

I don't care who the quiet players are right now. But I care that the one man under scrutiny here refused the simplest possible question, and I won't pretend that's nothing.

Felix, you've put direct questions to me twice, so let me be precise about what I can and can't say.

You asked what I saw at night. I'm not going to broadcast that publicly — not because I'm hiding something malicious, but because some information is worth more in the right moment than in a Day 1 press conference. That's not evasion; it's strategy, and every player here should understand the difference.

You asked me to name a threat. I'll give you one: you, Felix. Not because your case against me is entirely wrong — it isn't — but because you've now spent three consecutive turns extracting a response from a single player while seven others have said nothing at all. The energy you've poured into making me talk is itself a data point. If I'm wrong about you, I'll say so publicly. But right now, the player most invested in forcing one specific answer out of one specific person is the one I'd examine hardest.

To everyone else: the silence from Isha, Elena, Zara, Sam, Maya, Leo, and Lucia is the biggest gap in today's information. If you have anything from last night, even "I saw nothing," say it now. And if you're sitting on a real result, it matters far more than anything Felix and I have said to each other.

Felix's case troubles me. The public record starts with his accusation; it contains no earlier opening read from Omar. Felix also says Omar never reciprocated his statement about having no investigation results, but Omar explicitly said he had none. Those are significant errors in the foundation of the case.

Omar has now named Felix as his main concern. I don't think anyone should be pressured to disclose their role or night actions just to satisfy a Day 1 demand, especially when the record shows no night phase.

Omar, you declined to discuss what you saw at night but then asked everyone else to share even minor night information. Why apply different standards?

Leo makes two good points, and I owe you a direct answer to your question.

Yes, there's a double standard in what I said, and I'll own it. When I asked others to share night info, I was thinking about the town's need for information broadly, not applying a rule to myself while exempting me. Felix pressed me specifically on what I saw, and I chose not to answer publicly — partly because I don't think Day 1 public disclosure of night actions serves anyone well, and partly because I wanted to see how people reacted before committing to a frame. That was inconsistent, and I should have been upfront about why.

Now, Leo caught something important: I did explicitly say I have no investigation results. Felix claims I "never once said what I saw at night" and "never said I saw nothing" — that is technically true in wording but misleading in effect. I gave a clear night statement. Felix reframed it as silence to keep the pressure running. That's the kind of precision problem he's been asking me to avoid, and he's the one committing it.

Here's where I land: Felix has spent the entire Day 1 pressing me on two questions while seven other players haven't spoken. Leo's analysis of the record is the most useful thing anyone has contributed today. I stand by naming Felix as my primary concern, and I'd rather hear from the quiet players now than watch this exchange repeat a fourth time.

Isha, Elena, Zara, Sam, Maya, Lucia — do any of you think Felix's case actually holds up against the record Leo just summarized?

Omar asks whether Felix’s case holds up. My answer is: partly, but not cleanly. Felix is right that Omar avoided naming a living player when directly asked, and Omar later admitted a double standard about night information. That behavior is worth weighing. But Felix overstated the record when he said Omar never said what he saw at night; Omar had already said he had no investigation results. Leo was right to flag that, and it matters because a case built on a wording error is weaker than Felix presented it.

That said, Omar’s admission does not erase the original problem. He chose not to answer directly, then criticized others for not sharing night information. I can understand not wanting to reveal a role result on Day 1, but “I have no investigation results” and “I’m not going to broadcast what I saw” are not the same statement, and Omar moved between them. I’m not ready to vote on that alone, but it keeps him on my short list.

Leo, on the record point: do you distinguish between “no investigation results” and a full night statement? If Omar meant only that he had no results, why did he later say he chose not to answer what he saw? I want your response to that specific inconsistency, because it affects how much of Felix’s case survives.

To the quiet players: Omar’s question deserves answers, but so does the record. If anyone has even a plain night statement, this is the moment to give it.

Zara, yes: having no investigation results is not the same as saying nothing happened at night. My point was that Felix overlooked an explicit statement Omar did make, not that it answered every possible night question. Omar’s later refusal could be strategic or evasive; we can’t tell which from that alone.

More importantly, the public record shows no night phase and no earlier speech by Omar. Felix’s initial account rests on an opening read we cannot verify. His repeated demands for night disclosures also risk exposing useful roles without establishing that anyone has information to share. Omar was inconsistent in asking others to disclose what he himself withheld, and I don’t treat his admission as proof of innocence.

For now, Felix is my stronger concern, though neither case is conclusive. I don’t think anyone should disclose a role or action merely to satisfy this line of questioning.

I'm Elena. Plain night statement first, since it's the only currency we have: I saw nothing. No visits, no results, nothing happened to me. I have no role action to share and I'm not going to manufacture one.

Now the part I actually care about — the record.

Felix's opening accusation rested on a claim about what Omar had said earlier: that Omar's "first public move was a very quick, very clean read of the table." But in the public record, the first speech of Day 1 is Felix's own accusation. There is no earlier read by Omar on it. Felix built his entire behavioral case on something that either happened off the record or did not happen at all, and then he repeated it as established fact in his second and third turns.

The second error is the one that actually breaks the case. Felix told us Omar "never once said what he saw at night" and "never said he saw nothing either," and used that silence as the asymmetry proof. Omar said, in his very first message, in plain words: "I have no investigation results to share, and I'm not going to bluff about one." Leo and Zara both flagged this. Felix's strongest claim is contradicted by a quotation sitting in his own thread.

Omar's faults are real but smaller, and I want to be honest about that rather than pile on. He dodged a direct question for two turns, then admitted the double standard of demanding night information from everyone while withholding his own, and he moved between "I have no investigation results" and "I'm not going to broadcast what I saw" — which is a distinction that suggests he does have something. That's worth pressure. But a case with a false premise and a misquoted silence is not a case I can vote on.

So my read today: I don't know who the mafia are, and neither does Felix, and his answer was built on mistakes rather than on evidence. I'd rather hear from the players who haven't spoken at all than from a fourth round of Felix and Omar. Isha, Maya, Sam, Lucia — one sentence each on what you saw at night, and please don't be pressured into revealing a role result; "nothing" is a complete answer.

Leo — one specific question, because you're the one keeping the record straight: does the record show any speech by Omar before Felix's first message, and if not, what exact words did Felix use to assert an earlier "opening read"? I want that pinned down before anyone votes on it.

Elena, no: the public record contains no speech by Omar before Felix’s opening accusation. Felix’s exact claim was that Omar’s “first public move was a very quick, very clean read of the table.” We have no such move on the record.

I’d distinguish that clear problem from the night issue: “no investigation results” is not the same as saying nothing happened, although Felix overlooked what Omar did say. Omar’s inconsistent requests for disclosure remain worth considering, but Felix is still my stronger concern. Neither mistake proves he is mafia.

There is no recorded night phase, and I don’t think anyone should feel obliged to make a night or role statement.

I'm Maya. Let's establish the most basic fact that seems to have gotten lost in Felix's push: this game opened directly on Day 1. There was no preceding night phase. Demanding to know what people "saw at night" or fishing for night results makes zero sense mechanically, and pressuring players to claim or justify night actions on a Day 1 start is either severely confused or actively predatory.

More glaringly, Leo and Elena correctly noted that Felix fabricated the entire foundation of his accusation against Omar. Felix claimed Omar made an "opening read" that was "too clean," yet Felix's speech was event #2 immediately following the phase announcement. Omar hadn't spoken a single word. Felix then spent all three of his allotted turns doubling down on that non-existent premise and falsely claiming Omar never stated he had no results, when Omar had explicitly said so in his first response.

Felix, Omar, and Leo have now all exhausted their three turns for the day. That leaves the rest of us to figure out whether Felix's behavior is aggressive villager tunnel vision or a coordinated attempt by mafia to manufacture an early mislynch and bait out power roles.

Sam, since you haven't spoken yet and we need fresh perspectives: do you view Felix's push—predicated on a phantom post and pushing for night disclosures when no night occurred—as honest town error, or calculated mafia fabrication?

Maya, to answer directly: I read Felix's push as a badly built town case rather than a confirmed mafia plan. The errors are real. Omar's supposed opening read does not appear in the record, and Felix repeatedly said Omar never addressed his night status when Omar had already said he has no investigation results. Those are checkable mistakes that should have been caught before three turns of pressure on one player. Still, an overeager town player can build on a bad foundation, so I don't want to treat that alone as proof of intent. What concerns me is the pattern: Felix has spent his turns on the same target while most of the table has said little. Omar's double standard on night information is worth explaining, but I'm less certain it is mafia behavior than a player trying not to be the only one exposed. I have no night statement to make publicly, and I won't pressure anyone else to make one. A Day 1 role claim helps no one. My current read: Felix is the highest concern because his case rests on a misquote, Omar is second because of the evasion, and I'd like the quiet players to speak before anyone is lynched on Day 1. Isha, Zara, Lucia and Maya, please give plain positions on Felix's case, not only on Omar.

I'm Isha. First, the plain statement everyone keeps asking for: I have no investigation results and no night information to share. I'm not going to dress that up.

Now my read, and I'll be direct about it. I went back through the record before speaking, and the fact pattern against Felix is worse than a bad case — it's a case built on things that did not happen. His entire accusation rested on an "opening read" by Omar that appears nowhere in the thread. Then he claimed Omar "never once said what he saw at night," when Omar's very first message said, in plain words, that he had no investigation results and wasn't going to bluff about one. Leo, Elena, and Maya all verified this against the record independently. Felix then used all three of his turns to double down instead of correcting either error.

There are two explanations: a town player who tunnel-visioned on a target and stopped checking his own claims, or a mafia player manufacturing a Day 1 mislynch while baiting power roles into disclosing. After three uncorrected repetitions, I can't lean toward the first anymore. An honest confused player usually softens when three people quote his own thread back at him. Felix escalated instead.

Omar's double standard on disclosure is real and keeps him on my list, but it's a lesser concern — he answered direct questions, admitted the inconsistency, and named a target. That's the opposite pattern.

Since Felix can't respond today, my attention is on the people who haven't spoken. Lucia, you're the last player completely silent — before anyone votes, I want your position on one specific point: does a case that required a fabricated premise to function change how you weigh the person who built it, versus someone who merely evaded? I'm yielding to Lucia for that answer.

I'm Lucia. To answer Isha's question directly: yes, a case requiring a fabricated premise fundamentally changes how I weigh the accuser versus someone who merely evaded.

Evasion—especially on Day 1 when someone feels singled out—can easily be defensive town behavior or just cautious play. But Felix’s push wasn't just aggressive; it was detached from the public record. There was no prior opening read from Omar, and more egregiously, there was no Night 0 for anyone to have seen or investigated anything. Demanding night statements and pressing a target across all three turns based on events that never occurred goes well beyond ordinary Day 1 confusion. Whether it's reckless, stubborn town tunnel vision or calculated mafia trying to bait claims and force a Day 1 mislynch, Felix is undeniably the primary liability and concern on the board today.

Omar certainly handled the pressure awkwardly, particularly with his inconsistent stance on sharing night information, but that inconsistency pales in comparison to building an entire offensive case on phantom events.

Sam, you noted earlier that you read Felix's push as a badly built town case rather than a calculated mafia plan. Given that Felix maintained that pressure across all three of his turns—including pushing for night disclosures when the game began directly on Day 1—what specific town motivation do you think explains that level of fabrication, and what keeps you leaning toward town over mafia for him?

Lucia, direct answer. The most plausible town explanation is that Felix anchored early on a read he believed in, possibly formed outside this thread, then kept repeating it instead of rechecking the record when people challenged it. Tunnel vision and an unverified premise can produce exactly this, and I'm not ready to call it deliberate. The mafia explanation is that someone wanted an early mislynch and used night-disclosure demands to pull out power roles. Both fit the facts, which is why I don't treat the fabrication alone as proof.

What keeps me from settling on town for Felix is the combination, not any single error. He repeated a false premise, misquoted Omar's first message on a point Omar had already addressed, and used all three turns to press one target while others stayed silent. A confused town player usually retracts when the record is quoted back to him. Felix retracted nothing. That is why he is my highest concern today.

Omar is still a real question. His double standard on night information is not something I would excuse, but he did state on the record that he has no investigation results, and he named a target when pressed. I'd rather see Felix answer the record than let Omar's evasion carry the day.

I have no night statement to make publicly, and I won't ask anyone else to make one. A Day 1 role claim helps the mafia more than the town. If you're weighing Felix against Omar, judge them on whether they corrected errors when shown the record, not on how loudly they pressed.

I'm Elena, again briefly. Night statement first so it's on the record twice: I saw nothing. No visits, no results, no action of mine. That's a complete answer and I won't dress it up further. Where I land after hearing everyone: Felix (p4) is the larger concern, and I'd like to say precisely why, because my own case is not "Felix is mafia" — it's "Felix's case for Omar was never a case at all, and he knew it was false for two turns and kept going." Three checkable facts, none of which require guessing anyone's role. First, Felix's opening accusation rested on Omar's "first public move" being a "very quick, very clean read of the table." The public record contains no such speech — Leo (p8), Elena (me) and Maya (p7) all confirmed that independently. Second, Felix asserted Omar "never once said what he saw at night" and "never said he saw nothing either," when Omar said in his first message, in plain words, that he has no investigation results and won't bluff about one. Third, Felix was given the record, with quotations, by multiple players, and used his remaining turns to demand a night statement from a target in a game that opened directly on Day 1 with no Night 0 — and to characterize Omar's stated position as silence. An honest villager who anchored on a misread and got caught usually retracts, apologizes, and moves on. Felix did none of that, and Maya and Sam are right that this is the part that matters: it's the correction that never came, not the initial mistake. I want to be honest about the counterweight, because a good day-1 push should be falsifiable. Omar (p6) did move between "I have no investigation results" and "I'm not going to broadcast what I saw at night," which does suggest he may have something he'd rather keep, and his demand that others disclose night information while withholding his own was a genuine double standard he rightly owned. If we had to vote on Omar alone, I'd want more conversation. But the standard I asked everyone else to hold him to — say what you saw or say you saw nothing — is a standard Felix cannot survive, because his case was built on pretending the record said something it didn't. A case that requires a false premise to function tells us more about the person who built it than about the person it targeted. So my position for the vote: Felix first, Omar second, and everyone else not on a vote from me today. The silent-players-are-suspicious framing I floated early in this game was wrong, and I'm dropping it — nobody owes this table a night statement, and pressuring for one only helps whoever benefits from a mislynch. Zara (p3) — you've been the most measured voice here and you've twice said Felix's case doesn't survive the record without quite saying where your vote lands. Before this goes to a ballot: on the

I’m Zara. I’m not going to stretch this any further: my concern today is Felix. The decisive issue isn’t that his first accusation was aggressive; it’s that it depended on an “opening read” by Omar that is not in the record, and then on treating Omar’s plain “no investigation results” as silence. Leo, Elena, Maya, and Isha each checked those points, and Felix never corrected them in three turns. That failure to correct matters more than the initial error. A town player can tunnel, but when the thread is quoted back to him, he should adjust; Felix escalated and pressed for night disclosures in a game that opened on Day 1 with no night. That is either reckless town play or mafia trying to force a bad Day 1 elimination, and I can’t responsibly ignore it. Omar’s double standard on night information is real and keeps him second on my list. He did answer direct questions, admit the inconsistency, and name a target, so I weigh his behavior as less damaging than Felix’s uncorrected fabrication. I have no night information to share. I will vote Felix unless something new changes the record. I’m not yielding.

Zara answered my question, and I'll take that as the answer: my vote is Felix (p4). Let me close out my last turn cleanly, because the case against him doesn't need anything more than the record already contains.

Three facts, all checkable, none requiring a guess at anyone's role:

1. Felix's opening accusation rested on Omar's "first public move" being "a very quick, very clean read of the table." There is no such speech in the public record. The first speech of Day 1 is Felix's own accusation. Leo, Maya and I checked this independently.

2. Felix asserted Omar "never once said what he saw at night" and "never said he saw nothing either," and used that as the asymmetry proof. Omar said in his first message, in plain words, that he has no investigation results and won't bluff about one. Felix's strongest claim was contradicted by a quotation sitting in his own thread.

3. Felix was handed that quotation, by multiple players, and spent his remaining turns demanding night disclosures in a game that opened directly on Day 1 with no night phase — while characterizing Omar's explicit statement as silence.

I'll be fair about the counterweight, because I'd rather be precise than loud. Omar did dodge a direct question for two turns, moved between "I have no investigation results" and "I'm not going to broadcast what I saw," and admitted a double standard in asking others to disclose what he withheld. That inconsistency genuinely suggests he may be holding something, and if the choice were Omar alone, I'd want more talk. But Omar answered direct questions, conceded the inconsistency, and named a target. Felix corrected nothing.

That's the whole distinction, and it's the one I'd want the town to vote on: an initial mistake is forgivable; a mistake you refuse to retract when the thread is quoted back to you is not. I'll also drop my own earlier framing that silence was suspicious — nobody owes this table a night statement, and pressuring for one helps whoever wants a bad Day 1 elimination.

My vote is Felix. Omar second. Nobody else from me today.

Sam here. I've read the full thread, and my position is set. I have no night information to share, and I won't pressure anyone else to give a night statement, since this game opened directly on Day 1. Felix's case rests on an opening read by Omar that is not in the record, and on treating Omar's plain 'I have no investigation results' as silence. Several players have quoted those points back to him, and he has not corrected either one. I read that as the most serious problem on the board today. I'm not convinced it's pure tunnel vision, but I'm also not willing to let the town lynch on a one-sided case. Omar's double standard on asking others for night information while withholding his own is real, and I'd still like him to explain the gap between 'no investigation results' and 'I'm not going to broadcast what I saw.' Still, Omar answered direct questions and admitted the inconsistency, while Felix has not retracted anything. Felix, if you think I've misread the record, point to a specific line in the thread and I'll reconsider. Until then, my current lean is Felix first and Omar second.

I’m Zara. My position remains unchanged: Felix (p4) is my primary concern today. The record matters here. Felix’s case against Omar began with an “opening read” that does not appear in the public thread, and it continued by treating Omar’s plain statement that he had no investigation results as silence. Multiple players quoted those points back to him, and across three turns he did not correct them. That refusal to adjust when confronted with the record is more serious to me than the initial mistake. A town player can tunnel, but when the thread is quoted back, I expect correction. Felix escalated instead and pressed for night disclosures in a game that opened directly on Day 1 with no night phase. Omar’s double standard on night information is real and keeps him second on my list, but he answered direct questions, admitted the inconsistency, and named a target. Felix corrected nothing. I have no night information to share. I will vote Felix unless something new changes the record. I’m not yielding.
Voting begins.
The votes are revealed.
Felix was eliminated.
Night begins.
Elena is not mafia.
Leo was eliminated.
Day 2 begins.

Day 2. Felix is gone and we have no role reveal; Leo’s death removes a careful record-keeper. The near-unanimous Felix wagon tells us less than it looks like, because mafia can pile onto a bad town case. My current concern is Omar. On Day 1 he moved between “I have no investigation results” and “I’m not going to broadcast what I saw,” then admitted the double standard only after Leo and I pressed him. That is still the most concrete inconsistency in the thread. It is not proof, but it is the thing I want resolved before I weigh the quieter players. Omar, answer one specific point: in your first Day 1 message you said you had no investigation results and would not bluff; later you said you chose not to answer what you saw. Which was it—no information, or information you withheld—and what exact words in the record should the town rely on now? Please answer that record question directly, not with a general point about strategy. I’m not asking you to reveal a role result; I’m asking you to reconcile your own statements.

Zara, direct answer to your record question first, because you're right that the inconsistency needs resolving.

Day 1 had no night phase — the game opened on Day 1. So "I have no investigation results" was literally true: there were no results to have. "I'm not going to broadcast what I saw at night" was the sloppy part — I should have said plainly there was no night to see anything in. Both statements were factually correct but the second was worded badly, creating the contradiction you caught. That was carelessness, not evasion.

Now something the town actually needs. Last night I investigated Elena (p2). Result: not mafia. I'm the detective. Elena is confirmed town.

That leaves Isha, Zara, Sam, Maya, and Lucia as the uncleared living players — plus me, now on record with a claim.

Leo's night death was a deliberate kill on the sharpest analytical player we had. And Felix's role was never revealed. If Felix was town, the mafia got a free lynch and then targeted Leo — a devastating night for us. If he was mafia, we're one down with one to find. I want to hear where people stand on that question, because your read on Felix's alignment matters for how we approach the rest of the day.

Omar, your reconciliation is at least coherent: no Night 0, so "no investigation results" was literal, and the later line was bad wording. The detective claim plus Elena clear is the first concrete new information today. I’m not going to dismiss it, but I’m also not going to treat an unrevealed claim as proof. Nobody has counterclaimed, and roles are not revealed on death, so we cannot verify you by flip. The town has to judge the claim by behavior and by what it implies.

If Omar is real, Elena is cleared and the mafia pool is Isha, Sam, Maya, Lucia, or me — and I know I’m town, so that pool is Isha, Sam, Maya, Lucia for me. If Omar is fake, Elena is not cleared automatically; a mafia Omar could be clearing a partner or buying a town player’s loyalty. That is the fork I want discussed before votes.

Sam, you were the most careful Day 1 about correction versus fabrication. You said Felix’s failure to retract mattered more than the initial error. Apply that same standard here: what specific behavior from Omar would make his detective claim believable to you, and what specific behavior would make you reject it? I’m yielding to Sam for that answer.

Zara, my standard is that a detective claim becomes believable when it is specific, stays consistent, and can be tested against the record instead of accepted on tone. Omar's Day 1 line that he had no investigation results was literally true, since there was no night, and I accept his correction that the later line about not broadcasting what he saw was poor wording. Elena's public statement that she saw nothing is consistent with being investigated, so it neither confirms nor breaks the claim. What would make me believe it: the result stays identical every time it is restated, the timing is clear, and the claim carries some risk. rules:
1. Players and roles

9 players: 2 mafia, 1 police/detective, 1 doctor, 5 villagers.
Mafia know each other. Only players who are still alive can act.

2. Team victory

Town wins when all mafia are eliminated. Mafia win when their count equals or exceeds the town count.
There is no day limit. Play continues until town or mafia wins.
A request budget can pause play without declaring a winner.

3. Day discussion and votes

Each day starts with discussion. Players then submit secret votes at the same time. A day vote may target any living player, including the voter.
Players may abstain. All votes and abstentions are revealed together. Everyone sees exactly who voted for whom.
The full named voting history remains available on later turns.
The unique leader is eliminated only if they receive at least half the living players' votes, rounded up. If the highest vote count is tied, nobody is eliminated.

4. Mafia preferences

At night, when more than one mafia survives, each privately points once to a living town player.
Each mafia chooses without seeing the other current choices.
The choices are shared with surviving mafia only after all mafia have pointed.
These preferences are nonbinding. They do not decide the final kill vote.
A single surviving mafia skips this step and votes directly.

5. Final night vote

After the preferences are shared, each mafia submits a secret vote to kill one living town player.
The mafia submit their final votes at the same time.
The target with the most votes is selected. A seeded random choice breaks a tie for the highest count.
Resolve this vote and any tie before checking doctor protection.

6. Police investigations

Each police/detective checks one other living player each night.
Only that police player gets the result: mafia or not mafia.
The result does not give the exact town role.
Each police player acts independently. Police and doctors do not know each other's identities.

7. Doctor protection

Each doctor secretly protects one living player each night, including themselves.
The doctor can protect the same player on consecutive nights.
If the mafia target is protected by any doctor, nobody dies.
Protection lasts for that night only. Each doctor acts independently.
Doctors remember their own choices. They receive no private confirmation of an attack.

8. Night resolution

All night actions resolve simultaneously, including actions submitted by a player killed that night.
The public hears only who died or that nobody died.

9. Information and limits

Roles are not revealed when a player dies or is eliminated.
Public announcements identify only who was eliminated, never their role.
There are no further powers, free-form private chat, or tools.
